list.listitem: Physical examination (groin pain/bulge with a palpable mass) is a reliable means to diagnose an inguinal hernia. C
Ultrasound or MRI imaging may be used to confirm the diagnosis but is usually not necessary. C

Options for surgical repair include open or laparoscopic surgery (i.e., transabdominal preperitoneal and totally extraperitoneal repairs). Both open and laparoscopic repair offer similar rates of recurrence and most postoperative complications and length of hospital stay. A Laparoscopic repair is associated with lower rates of postoperative and chronic pain and a 1-day shorter average return to work. B
Use of several different preoperative medications or intraoperative nerve blocks can reduce postoperative pain. A
Recurrence rates following surgery range from 10.5% to 11.4% for men and 6.2% to 7.1% for women, although it is not clear that recurrence rates differ by gender. A

Use of mesh results in lower recurrence rates for open procedures but is not clearly shown to make a difference for laparoscopic procedures . Heavyweight mesh may reduce recurrence risk during laparoscopic surgery, B but lightweight mesh may reduce post-operative pain. B Glue mesh fixation appears to have an advantage with respect to less early chronic pain which did not differ between groups at 24 months. A

Men older than 18 years may safely elect to observe minimally symptomatic hernias, data on women are scant. The complication rate is 1.8/1000 patient years. B Watchful waiting prevents surgery in between 1/4 and 3/4 of patients at 1 to 10 years without increasing risk of complications from surgery. B

background.definition: An abdominal wall hernia results from protrusion of abdominal contents through a weakness or defect in the wall; about 75% of abdominal wall hernias are inguinal.

list.listitem: About 700,000 inguinal hernia repairs are performed annually in the United States.

In a population study from Olmsted County, MN, from 1989 to 2008, there were 4026 inguinal hernia repairs performed on 3599 adults for an incidence rate of 368 per 100,000 person-years for men and 44 per 100,000 person-years for women. The lifelong cumulative incidence of an initial inguinal hernia repair in adulthood was 42.5% in men and 5.8% in women.
No data are available regarding asymptomatic hernias or hernias for which the patient does not seek surgical repair.
About 24% of men and 5% of women will develop an inguinal hernia in their lifetime.
Inguinal hernia appears to be a risk factor for abdominal aortic aneurism.

Females appear to have more occult femoral hernias identified during surgery for inguinal hernia and are at higher risk for having a femoral hernia identified during reoperation for inguinal hernia repair than males (RR 9, 95% CI 7.4, 10.9).

Among patients with groin hernia incarceration, 21% required bowel resection based on a meta-analysis of 7 studies with 762 patients. Risk factors for bowel resection in the pooled analysis were female, age >65 years, femoral hernia, bowel obstruction, duration of incarceration (hours), white blood cell count, and neutrophilic leukocyte count.
Most inguinal hernias are caused by a congenital dysfunction in the closure of the abdominal wall.
Other rare congenital defects exist, such as defects in collagen formation.

Authors of a meta-analysis found that a positive family history increased the risk of inguinal hernia in children and adults (OR 5.3, 95% CI 3.3-8.7 for adults). Among adults, the highest risk of inguinal hernia repair occurred when a sister had been repaired compared with a brother.

Ancestry-specific inguinal hernia susceptibility loci have been identified that are specific to men and women and for those of African origin. In one meta-analysis, five studies revealed 92 susceptible loci across 66 genes, predominantly linked to immune responses for inguinal hernia. Elevated MMP-2 levels were reported in 11 studies, with greater MMP-2 levels found in direct compared to indirect inguinal hernias.
Smoking and drug use, including steroids, are associated and may be consider acquired or contributing causes.
The effects of straining or heavy lifting remain controversial.
Among men undergoing radical prostatectomy, there appears to be a higher mean prevalence of inguinal hernia after robotic-assisted prostatectomy compared to a laparoscopic procedure.
Indirect inguinal hernias originate at the internal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric artery.
Direct hernias arise through a weakness in the inguinal canal medial to this artery through Hesselbach's triangle.

Pain associated with inguinal hernia appears to be due to ilioinguinal nerve compression neuropathy as demonstrated by a study reporting increased preoperative pain scores correlated with increased nerve diameter, increased fascicle count and increased myxoid material within the perineurium and endoneurium.

Incarceration occurs when abdominal contents are trapped within the hernia defect. Strangulation occurs when the incarceration impedes blood flow inducing edema and possible ischemia, necessitating prompt surgical intervention.

list.listitem: It is common practice, especially in males, to evaluate the inguinal canal during a routine physical examination. However, there is no evidence that outcomes are improved by identifying occult hernias before they become symptomatic. C
Physical examination is specific, yet somewhat insensitive, in diagnosing an inguinal hernia. C
Ultrasound or MRI imaging can be used to confirm the diagnosis if necessary but is not routinely recommended. C

Neck of femoral hernia lies inferior to pubic tubercle
Only preperitoneal fat through inguinal ring

list.listitem: A careful history and physical examination can accurately diagnose most inguinal hernias. The examination can be more challenging in obese patients or patients who have had previous surgery. The physical examination is moderately sensitive and very specific; an abnormal examination is very strong evidence in favor of hernia, but a normal examination in a patient with persistent symptoms does not completely rule it out.
Patients typically present with a reducible mass in the groin, which may or may not be painful. The mass may arise suddenly or progress slowly over time, and may be unilateral or bilateral.

Examination involves a manual attempt to reduce the mass, and palpation of the abdominal wall defect to estimate its size. In men, the examiner should attempt to follow the spermatic cord cephalad to the external ring of the inguinal canal. With Valsalva induced by coughing or straining, it may be easier to evaluate for weakness in the abdominal wall.
A nonreducible mass raises the suspicion for incarceration.

Routine confirmation with imaging is usually not necessary. The American College of Radiology (2022) recommends ultrasound of the pelvis, MRI of pelvis without and with contrast, or CT of pelvis with or without abdominal CT and without or with contrast as usually appropriate for suspected groin hernia when confirmation is needed.

Herniography (hernia imaging after it has been injected with a contrast medium) in cases of occult inguinal hernia has good test characteristics with a sensitivity of 91% and a specificity of 83%. Interestingly, in a case series on use of herniography, of 72/204 patients with positive herniograms, only about half underwent surgery and six patients were found not to have a hernia at operation.

In two meta-analyses, sonography had an overall sensitivity of 86% to 96.6% and specificity of 77% to 84.8% for inguinal hernia. It should be considered for cases with diagnostic uncertainty. In the latter study, sensitivity of MRI at 80% was lower than that of ultrasound; MRI specificity was 65%.

In one case series of 30 children, ultrasound was used successfully to identify a patent processus vaginalis on the contralateral side of children undergoing unilateral hernia repair. The defect was confirmed and repaired in 11 of the 12 cases with a positive ultrasound.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 14 studies with 2120 children undergoing unilateral inguinal hernia repair found preoperative ultrasonography for non-clinically detected contralateral inguinal hernia to have a pooled sensitivity and specificity of 93% and 88%, respectively, using surgical exploration as the reference test (LR+ 7.8, LR- 0.08).
MRI in other studies was somewhat more sensitive but only minimally more specific than ultrasound.
Typical symptoms include groin pain or sense of bulging associated on physical examination with the presence of a hernia, which may or may not be reducible.

If not reducible, look for evidence of strangulation (severe pain, unstable vital signs and fever, abdominal findings suggesting peritonitis or small bowel obstruction). Any suspicion of strangulation of a nonreducible hernia is considered a surgical emergency.
Imaging options for unclear physical findings include ultrasound, MRI or CT as noted above.

For patients with asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic inguinal hernias, watchful waiting is a reasonable approach. Authors of a meta-analysis of 9 studies, including 3 RCTs, found conversion rates to elective surgery of between 35% and 58% and there were no significant statistical differences between watchful waiting and surgical repair for postoperative complications or hernia recurrence. Only one Turkish non-randomized study included women. (See section on "Other treatment" for additional information)

In adult patients undergoing surgical repair, simultaneous repair of a contralateral asymptomatic hernia, identified in about 22% of patients, does not increase hospital length of stay, complications or return to activities of daily living based on a meta-analysis of 6 nonrandomized studies with 978 patients. Patients undergoing bilateral repair had slightly longer mean operating times (mean 14.57 minutes) and higher postoperative pain scores. (See section on prognosis for additional information)

Surgical repair is the usual treatment of choice. Both open and laparoscopic repair offer similar rates of recurrence and most postoperative complications, and length of hospital stay. A Laparoscopic repair is associated with lower postoperative and chronic pain rates and a 1-day shorter average return to work. B

Minimally invasive procedures (laparoscopic transabdominal preperitoneal repair and totally extraperitoneal repair) are associated with significantly reduced early postoperative pain, return to work/activities, chronic pain, hematoma, and wound infection compared to the Lichtenstein tension-free repair, but data are conflicting. B
Use of several different preoperative medications or intraoperative nerve blocks can reduce postoperative pain. A

Use of mesh results in lower recurrence rates for open procedures but was not shown to make a difference for laparoscopic procedures based on one meta-analysis of 13 RCTs; lightweight mesh may have an advantage for reducing later postoperative pain and discomfort. A
Asymptomatic and minimally symptomatic inguinal hernias in men may be observed, data on women are scant. B

Authors of a Cochrane review of 17 trials found that antibiotic prophylaxis results in an approximately 1% absolute reduction in the risk of postoperative infection (NNT = 100); they concluded that routine use could not be universally recommended. Investigators in one RCT found a greater absolute reduction in surgical-site infection from use of antibiotic prophylaxis after open tension-free inguinal hernia (2% vs. 13% in the placebo group).

A benefit of prophylactic antibiotics for tension-free inguinal hernia repair was also found by authors of a meta-analysis who reported a reduced total incidence of surgical site infections and superficial surgical site infections in the antibiotic group compared to the non-antibiotic group, but no significant difference in the total incidence of postoperative infections or deep surgical site infections.

Authors of another meta-analysis of 15 RCTs found that β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitors and first-generation cephalosporins significantly reduced surgical site infections compared to placebo (risk ratio 0.44; 95% CI 0.25-0.75 and 0.62; 95% CI 0.42-0.92 respectively). There were no significant differences by antibiotic class.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs with 456 patients found that prophylactic alpha-blockade reduced rates of urinary retention requiring catheterization following elective inguinal hernia surgery primarily in men (3.7% vs. 24.3%, respectively) regardless of use of general or spinal anesthesia. Complication rates were similar.

Gabapentin (optimal dose 400 mg) administered orally 2 hours before surgery reduced first analgesic use and total opioid consumption within 24 hours after surgery compared to placebo in an RCT of 120 men undergoing inguinal herniorrhaphy under subarachnoid block.

Methocarbamol, a skeletal muscle relaxant, was found in a retrospective case-control study among patients undergoing primary ventral and inguinal hernia repair to reduce prescribed opioids (55.8% vs 90.4%) and lower morphine milligram equivalents (MME, 20 vs 50), with no difference in refills or rescue opioids.

IV dexamethasone 0.5 mg/kg plus caudal block was more effective than caudal block alone in reducing postoperative pain in the first 4 hours following inguinal hernia repair in an RCT of 64 children aged 1-5 years.

In an RCT of 64 children undergoing unilateral inguinal hernia repair, clonidine as an adjuvant to caudal bupivacaine prolonged the duration of analgesia (520 ± 57 minutes vs. 264 ± 69 minutes for caudal bupivacaine alone) without increasing adverse effects.

Field block with or without wound infiltration, either as a sole anesthetic/analgesic technique or as an adjunct to general anesthesia, can be used to reduce postoperative pain; continuous local anesthetic infusion of a surgical wound can be used to provide longer duration analgesia.
In one RCT, ultrasound-guided blocks of the ilioinguinal and iliohypogastric nerves resulted in reduced postoperative pain scores but not reduced use of opioids.

In an RCT of 60 patients undergoing inguinal hernia repair under general anesthesia, use of a transversus abdominis plane block with either ropivacaine 0.75% 20 mL or placebo 20 mL resulted in significantly less pain at rest and on movement and less morphine use during the hospital stay; 6-month pain results were comparable.

In another RCT of 92 patients undergoing inguinal hernia repair, those receiving perineural bupivacaine infiltration in addition to percutaneous ilioinguinal nerve block had less recovery room pain, shorter recovery discharge times (89 vs. 105 min), consumed fewer narcotics (9.7 vs. 15.1 doses), and reported less inguinodynia at 3 months compared to those receiving nerve block alone.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 6 studies with 632 patients comparing ilioinguinal/iliohypogastric nerve block to transversus abdominis plane block for pain management after inguinal hernia repair found no statistically significant differences between these approaches in postoperative opioid use, time to first request for rescue analgesia, incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting, incidence of complication related with nerve blocks, and patient satisfaction.

In an RCT of 72 patients undergoing open mesh inguinal hernioplasty, subarachnoid block (SAB) combined with continuous postoperative analgesia via a transverse abdominis plane catheter provided better pain control and functional outcome based on the Core Outcome Measures Index at 6 months than either SAB alone or general anesthesia.

In 40 patients undergoing unilateral inguinal hernia repair under general anesthesia, a quadrates lumborum block using a transmuscular approach was more effective than the posterior approach for postoperative analgesia.

There is controversy about the superiority of transversus abdominis plane block over quadratus lumborum block for adult patients undergoing inguinal hernia repair. Authors of a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs including 255 patients found quadratus lumborum block was associated with a significant decrease in postoperative pain (MD -0.45, 95% CI -0.75 to -0.14; I2 = 94%) but no difference in 24-hour opioid consumption, while another meta-analysis including 6 RCTs found low to moderate-quality preliminary evidence suggesting no difference in analgesic efficacy between the two blocks.
Refer to a surgeon to discuss open versus laparoscopic surgical repair. Options for laparoscopic surgery include transabdominal preperitoneal (TAPP) approach and totally extraperitoneal (TEP) repair.

Based on the Danish Hernia Database (recording over 10,000 inguinal hernias annually), recommendations are to use open surgery or laparoscopic repair for men, irrespective of age, laparoscopic repair for women and mesh repair for asymptomatic female and for symptomatic men and women with primary unilateral or bilateral groin hernia.

A retrospective cohort of men from the US VA system compared open repair with local anesthesia (n=22,333 patients), open repair with general anesthesia (n=75,104) and laparoscopic repair with general anesthesia (n=9636). In these cohorts undergoing unilateral primary inguinal repair there was not significant difference in outcomes.
Operative Anesthesia (also see peripheral nerve block section above)

Paravertebral block for operative anesthesia compared favorably with general anesthesia/systematic analgesia with reduced postoperative nausea and vomiting, and performed similarly to neuraxial block and other peripheral nerve blocks with less postoperative nausea and urinary retention than neuraxial blocks and less postoperative pain compared to other blocks.
Spinal anesthesia reduced immediate postoperative pain and pain at 8 hours compared to general anesthesia in a RCT of 70 adults with laparoscopic hernia repair by using a TAPP approach.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 11 RCTs of open inguinal hernia repair in adults, including 591 cases receiving local anesthesia and 584 cases receiving spinal anesthesia, found those undergoing local anesthesia had a lower incidence of headache (RR=0.11, 95% CI: 0.03, 0.46), urinary retention (RR=0.13, 95% CI: 0.05, 0.32) and postoperative pain score at 12 hours (SMD=-1.09, 95% CI: -1.41, -0.76), and a higher satisfaction rate (RR=1.12, 95% CI: 1.01, 1.24). There were no differences in operation time or the incidence of intraoperative pain, hematoma, infection, or postoperative chronic pain.
There is no difference in the risk of post-operative wound infection or wound hematoma with use of spinal vs. general anesthesia for patients undergoing TEP herniorrhaphy based on 7 RCTs.

Prophylactic ilioinguinal neurectomy significantly reduced groin pain at 1 and 6 months compared to nerve preservation following Lichenstein hernioplasty. Authors of a meta-analysis of 16 RCTs confirmed the benefit of ilioinguinal neurectomy following Lichenstein hernioplasty on short-term groin pain without increasing groin paresthesia at 6 months but no difference in chronic groin pain at 12 months (9% [9/100] in the neurectomy group versus 17.8% [20/112] in the inguinal nerve preservation group [RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.24-1.05]).

Use of ilioinguinal neurectomy also reduced postoperative pain in the first month and at 6 months compared to nerve preservation in open tension-free inguinal hernia repair based on a meta-analysis of RCTs. There was no difference between groups in the incidence of severe pain in the first month and patients undergoing neurectomy had a higher incidence of numbness in the first month postoperatively but not at 6 months.

Authors of a network meta-analysis of 31 studies with 11,683 patients found a significantly lower risk of urinary retention with use of local compared to general or regional anesthesia (crude rates 0.1%, 95% CI 0 to 0.2; 8.6%, 95% CI 6.6 to 10.5; and 1.4%, 95% CI 0.6 to 2.2, respectively) and lower risk with general compared to regional anesthesia.

In an RCT of 149 patients undergoing inguinal hernioplasty, use of conscious sedation with local anesthesia resulted in less pain experience and severity greater patient satisfaction compared to local anesthesia alone.

Of the open repair techniques, authors of a Cochrane review of 16 trials found the recurrence rate with Shouldice techniques to be lower than for other non-mesh techniques (OR 0.62; 95% CI 0.45-0.85). However, in the most recent meta-analysis of 14 RCTs including 2784 patients Shouldice was associated with a significant increase in recurrence rate (4.2% vs. 0.9%; RR 3.7, 95% CI 2.0-6.6; I2 = 0%) compared with Lichtenstein.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 3 trials comparing an open preperitoneal technique to the Lichtenstein open tension-free mesh inguinal hernia repair found similar low recurrence rates and a trend towards less chronic pain using the preperitoneal technique. However, authors of a meta-analysis of 10 RCTs and 2 comparison studies found that the open preperitoneal technique was associated with a lower recurrence rate than the Lichtenstein repair, while another meta-analysis of 12 small RCTs found the procedures comparable. In another RCT, there was less chronic pain experienced at 1 year by patients undergoing preperitoneal mesh positioning vs. the Lichtenstein repair.

In an RCT of 812 patients using 1 of 3 open techniques - Lichtenstein's, Trabucco's sutureless technique and Valenti two self-regulating prostheses technique - performed under local anesthesia by surgical residents, there were no differences in most early outcomes except for less operative time for the Trabucco group vs. Lichtenstein group and more pain on day 3 in the Valenti group vs. Lichtenstein group.

In a case series reporting on 9-year follow-up of 371 of 558 (65%) inguinal hernia repairs, the recurrence rate was 2.2% with no differences between Valenti and Lichtenstein repairs; 4 patients in each group reported constant pain and severe pain was reported by 1.6% and 2.1%, respectively.

The performance of open or laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair by supervised resident physicians does not appear to be associated with a higher risk of reoperation for recurrence compared with operations performed by specialists based on a nationwide register-based Danish cohort study including 31,683 primary groin and 7777 primary ventral hernia repairs.
Based on a retrospective cohort study of 400 patients, outcomes were similar for lightweight polypropylene mesh (34-36 gm/m2) and heavy weight polypropylene mesh (95 gm/m2).

Of the laparoscopic techniques, TEP repair and TAPP repair have equivalent operative times, postoperative complications, postoperative pain, time to return to work, and recurrence rates. These data were based on an indirect comparison of meta-analyses of the two procedures against open repair in 2012. In a Swiss population analysis of over 4500 cases comparing the two procedures, however, intraoperative and surgical postoperative complications were significantly lower in patients undergoing TAPP.

Authors of a Cochrane review update including 23 RCTs comparing TAPP and TEP laparoscopic techniques for inguinal hernias found little to no difference between the procedures for serious adverse events, hernia recurrence, or chronic pain based on low- to very-low-certainty evidence. They found a possible increase in need to convert from TEP to TAPP or open surgery when compared to the risk of needing to convert from TAPP to open surgery (low-certainty evidence).

Closure of direct hernia defects is not routine in laparoscopic direct hernioplasty. Authors identified 4 studies, two of which demonstrated reduced rates of recurrence with closure vs. non-closure of the medial hernia defect while the remaining two studies reported no recurrences with either approach. Two studies also reported a reduced incidence of post-operative seroma formation with closure.

Robotic TAPP repair was successful in 99.4% of patients, with short-term recurrence (maximum 368 days) reported in 0.18% (95% CI 0.00-0.84%) based on a meta-analysis of 12 studies with 1645 patients. Operative time ranged from 45 to 180.4 minutes, intraoperative complications occurred in 0.03% (95% CI 0.0-0.3) and conversion in 0.14% (95% CI 0.0-0.5%). Estimated pooled prevalence of urinary retention, seroma/hematoma, and overall complications were 3.5% (95% CI 1.6-5.8%), 4.1% (95% CI 1.6-7.5%), and 7.4% (95% CI 3.4-10.9%).

Similar findings were reported in a meta-analysis including 2521 patients undergoing robotic inguinal hernia repairs; overall average operative time was 90.8 min (range 25-180.7 min), overall conversion rate was 0.63%, overall complication rate was 10.1%, overall recurrence rate was 1.2% (14/1218) and readmission rate was 1.6%.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 10 studies comparing robot-assisted TAPP respair to laparoscopic TAPP repair for inguinal hernia found no statistically significant differences in complications or recurrence rates, but robotic procedures had longer operative times (MD = 14 minutes) and higher costs (MD = $4.17 thousand).

list.listitem: Authors of a network meta-analysis of 31 RCTs found no differences in hernia recurrence, chronic pain, hematoma, seroma, or hospital stays between TAPP, TEP, and Lichtenstein repairs for inguinal hernias. TAPP and TEP decreased return-to-work days by about 1 day. Authors of a meta-analysis of 35 RCTs with 7777 patients undergoing inguinal hernia repair found minimally-invasive TAPP and TEP repair seemed associated with significantly reduced early postoperative pain, return to work/activities, chronic pain, hematoma, and wound infection compared to the Lichtenstein tension-free repair, with no differences in seroma formation, hernia recurrence, or hospital length of stay.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 12 RCTs of variable methodologic quality with 3966 patients undergoing mesh repair of unilateral inguinal hernia found no significant differences in recurrence rates between the laparoscopic and Lichtenstein (open) groups (OR 1.14, 95% CI 0.51-2.55). Laparoscopic repair was associated with a reduced rate of acute pain compared to open repair and reduced odds of chronic pain compared to open repair (OR 0.41, CI 0.30-0.56).

Similarly, authors of a meta-analysis of 58 RCTs found laparoscopic repair associated with significantly less early (2 weeks to 6 months) and late postoperative pain and higher patient satisfaction compared to open repair.

Long-term follow-up of 83.1% of 302 original patients participating in the TULIP trial comparing transinguinal preperitoneal (TIPP) inguinal hernia repair with the Lichtenstein method found no difference between the groups in hernia recurrence rate, which was 2.8% overall, and no difference in chronic groin pain at a median follow-up of 85 months, only 1 patient out of 25 patients who reported pain at 1 year postop.

In one RCT comparing open and laparoscopic repairs, patients undergoing laparoscopic TAPP repair had better quality of life outcomes at a median follow-up of 17.9 months than patients undergoing open repair.

In another RCT of 416 patients, TEP and Lichtenstein inguinal hernia repair had similar outcomes at 1 year, with high rates of patient satisfaction (98.3%) and low rates of chronic pain (6.9% and 9.8% respectively) and recurrence (4 patients and 2 patients, respectively). Short-term advantages for pain and recovery rate were reported after TEP repair.

In an RCT of 134 patients undergoing surgery for bilateral inguinal hernia, TAPP repair resulted in less early postoperative pain up to 7 days and less chronic pain, a shorter hospital length of stay, and fewer postoperative complications compared to an open Lichtenstein repair.

In a meta-analysis of 19 studies, comparing 2521 patients undergoing robotic surgery with 4248 patients undergoing open repairs, the robotic group had significantly longer operative times but fewer readmission rates and no differences between the two groups for complications, post-operative pain or hernia recurrence. Comparing robotic surgery with 1495 patients undergoing laparoscopic repair, the robotic group had significantly longer operative times but fewer complications and no difference in post-operative pain occurrence, hernia recurrence rates or readmission rates. In another meta-analysis comparing laparoscopic surgery to robotic, costs were higher with robotic surgery by a mean of $3270.

Authors of a systematic review of 20 trials comparing open mesh with open nonmesh repair found that open mesh procedures reduce the risk of recurrence and may result in less persistent pain. A second Cochrane review also confirmed that Shouldice techniques during open repair had higher risk of recurrence than with mesh techniques (OR 3.80; 95% CI 1.99-7.26); few women, however, were included in these trials.

For emergency repair of incarcerated or strangulated groin hernia, mesh-based repair reduced recurrence (OR 0.4, 95% CI 0.2, 0.7; I2 = 35%) and length of hospital stay (OR - 1.0, 95% CI - 1.9, - 0.2; I2 = 94%) without increasing surgical site infection, mortality or postoperative complications based on a meta-analysis of 20 observational studies and 4 RCTs including 12,402 patients. However, in a subgroup analysis of patients who also underwent bowel resection, mesh repair was associated with an increased risk of surgical site infection (OR 1.7, 95% CI 1.04, 2.9; I2 = 9%).

For laparoscopic repair of groin hernias, authors of a meta-analysis of 13 RCTs with 1731 patients found no differences between mesh fixation using stapler or tacker and non-mesh procedures for recurrence rates, overall complications, length of hospital stay and time to resume normal activities. Post-operative visual analog pain scores were higher and operative time longer with mesh fixation.

For patients undergoing laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair with mesh, nonfixation technique compared to mesh fixation reduced rates of urinary retention, mean operative time, and postoperative pain at 24 hours and at 6 months with comparable rates of recurrence based on a meta-analysis of 18 trials including 2617 patients.

Authors of a systematic review of 21 RCTs concluded that prevalence of chronic pain was similar after mesh and non-mesh repairs with a median of median 2.9% (0%-27.6%) and 3.5% (0%-16.2%), respectively.

Lightweight mesh appears to be as effective as heavy mesh with respect to recurrence and reduces the incidence of chronic groin pain (RR 0.64; 95 % CI 0.51-0.82). Two-year results were comparable, however, in one large RCT with 950 patients. Authors of a meta-analysis of 21 RCTs with 4576 patients undergoing open (Lichtenstein) surgery for uncomplicated inguinal hernias found no differences between lightweight and heavyweight mesh for recurrence or severe pain at 3 to 60 months; lightweight mesh vs. heavyweight was associated with reduced rates of any pain (14.6% vs. 19.1%; RR 0.78; 95% CI 0.64-0.96) and for the feeling of a foreign body (12.3% vs. 20.2%; RR 0.64; 95% CI 0.51-0.80).

Conversely, in a meta-analysis of 12 RCTs of laparoscopic surgery for inguinal hernia repair, lightweight mesh increased the recurrence risk compared to heavyweight mesh (32/1571 vs. 13/1508; RR 2.21, CI 1.14-4.31), especially in non-fixated mesh direct repairs and/or large hernia defects. There were no differences in pain or foreign-body sensation by type of mesh.

In a meta-analysis of 12 RCTs and 5 cohort studies, self-gripping mesh performed similarly to conventional suture fixed Lichtenstein technique with respect to post-operative pain or chronic pain, complications, or recurrence. During laparoscopic repair, self-gripping mesh was associated with a lower incidence of chronic pain compared to conventional mesh (OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.20, 0.93) but there were no significant differences in hernia recurrence, hematoma or seroma formation in a meta-analysis of 4 RCTs and 1 prospective study. However, another meta-analysis of 14 studies with 3180 patients found no benefit on chronic pain comparing self-gripping to standard mesh.

Use of biologic Inguinal Hernia Matrix compared favorably with polypropylene mesh at 1-year follow-up with similar rates of recurrence and complications, based on a single trial of 100 men with inguinal hernia.

Glue mesh fixation compared with sutures is associated with shorter operative times, less postoperative pain, earlier return to daily activities, and comparable hernia recurrence rates; In the most recent RCT of 331 patients, the incidence of chronic postoperative pain was 7.3% at 3 months and 4.6% at 24 months and did not differ between self-gripping or sutured mesh groups.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 17 RCTs with 3150 hernias found no significant difference between glue and suture mesh fixation in postoperative seroma, chronic pain after 1 year or early or late recurrence. In a network meta-analysis, fibrin glue fixation was superior to non-absorbable sutures (RR 0.23, 95% credibility interval [95%CrI] 0.09, 0.50), absorbable sutures (RR 0.24, 95%CrI 0.08, 0.60), chemical glue (RR 0.36, 95%CrI 0.13, 0.87), and self-gripping mesh (RR 0.27, 95%CrI 0.09, 0.62) for preventing chronic pain of >3 months.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 13 RCTS found mesh fixation with glue resulted in less early chronic pain and hematoma formation and shorter operative times by about 4 minutes than closure with sutures in Lichtenstein repair inguinal hernia without increasing recurrence rates.

With respect to wound drains following laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair, authors of a meta-analysis of 16 studies involving 4369 patients, found a lower incidence of seroma formation in the drainage tube group compared to the non-drainage tube group (OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.07-0.353) but no differences in hospital stay, blood loss or recovery time.

Absorbable suture use in inguinal hernia repair was associated with a lower rate of chronic pain (absolute difference 2.2%) and a shorter time to pain resolution compared with nonabsorbable sutures in one RCT.

Recommendations to reduce the risk of chronic groin pain from the International Consensus Conference were to identify and preserve all three inguinal nerves during open inguinal hernia repair and to electively resect a suspected injured nerve. Authors of a meta-analysis found a pooled mean difference in degree of pain at 6 months postoperatively of only −0.29 on a 10-point scale (95% CI −0.48 to −0.11) for planned resection of the ilioinguinal nerve at the time of inguinal hernia repair vs. no resection.

Fenugreek transdermal patch 10% twice daily was more effective than placebo patch for management of inguinal hernia post-operative pain up to 24 hours postoperatively in a small RCT and performed better than diclofenac dermal patch 1% at 1 and 6 hours. The diclofenac dermal patch was also better than placebo from 6-24 hours postoperatively
Watchful waiting is a viable option for asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic inguinal hernias in men.

In 1 study, 720 men older than 18 years with minimally symptomatic inguinal hernias were followed for 4.5 years after randomization to 2 groups: watchful waiting and elective repair. Both groups had similar quality of life, pain, and complication rates. Overall, the complication rate of clinically significant incarceration was 1.8/1000 patient years in the watchful waiting group.
In another study of 336 patients randomized to watchful waiting, 72 patients crossed over to surgery at 2 years and 28 patients developed pain, limiting their activities.

In the most recent RCT of 496 men aged 50 years and older with mildly symptomatic or asymptomatic inguinal hernia, at 2 years follow-up 93 patients (35.4%) in the watchful waiting group underwent elective surgery and 6 (2.3%) received emergent surgery for strangulation/incarceration. Mean pain scores were higher in the watchful waiting group, but postoperative complication rates and recurrence rates in the 99 operated individuals were comparable with individuals originally assigned to the elective repair group (8.1% vs 15.0%).

Information from longer follow up ranging from 3.2 to 12 years from 3 RCTs including 592 participants found a crossover rate to surgery of 54.2% (95% CI 45.5% - 66.3%) with cumulative 1-year, 5-year, and 10- year crossover rates of 28.7%, 51.5% and 70.6% (95% CI 66.2% - 74.9%), respectively. The most frequent reasons for crossover to herniorrhaphy were pain 198/344 (57.6%) and incarceration 15/344 (4.4%).
Hospitalization and urgent surgical intervention are recommended for patients with evidence of incarceration or strangulation of abdominal contents.
This occurs at an annual risk of 3 per 1000 patients with hernia.
In men with minimally symptomatic inguinal hernia, complications are rare (1.8/1000 patients/year).

Postoperative urinary retention after elective inguinal hernia repair occurred in about 6% of male patients (n = 224) and 3% of female patients (n = 8) in an international prospective cohort study in which most (82%) patients underwent open procedures. Risk factors were increasing age, anticholinergic medication, history of urinary retention, constipation, out-of-hours surgery, involvement of urinary bladder within the hernia, temporary intraoperative urethral catheterization, and increasing operative duration.

Chronic postoperative inguinal pain occurs in about 17% of patients, although the lowest reported incidence was from trials in North America (6.0%, 95%CI 4.6 ~ 7.6). Risk factors for chronic pain in this meta-analysis of 18 studies included younger age, female, presence of other postoperative complications, hernial sac defect <3 cm, reporting perioperative and postoperative, and having a history of ipsilateral inguinal hernia repair. Another study found similar risk factors for chronic postoperative pain, including recurrent hernia.

With respect to chronic pain, authors of a meta-analysis of 22 RCTs comparing laparoscopic to open inguinal hernia repair found decreasing pain in all groups over time with rates of 4.7% and 6.9%, respectively, at >5 years; overall chronic pain rates were lowest with TEP. However, there was no difference between techniques when pain was described as moderate and/or affecting daily activities.

Chronic neuropathic pain after groin surgery can be treated with neurectomy of the iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal and genitofemoral nerves. Authors of a meta-analysis of 5 studies including 142 patients found a minimally invasive endoscopic method of neurectomy was up to 78% effective (95% CI 71%, 84%).

Pain-related impairment of sexual function is a potential complication; in one RCT, new pain occurred in 8% of 259 patients at 6 months following inguinal hernia repair. Those randomized to the Onstep technique appeared to have lower rates of pain than those undergoing the Lichtenstein technique (7/130 vs. 14/129).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 12 studies of inguinal hernia repair in 4884 adults, followed for a median of 10.5 months, found incidence rates of new-onset, postoperative sexual dysfunction with minimally invasive surgery of 7.8% (95% CI 5.4% to 11.3%) and with open repair 3.7% (95% CI 2.0% to 6.8%). For pain with sexual activity, respective rates were 7.4% (95% CI 4.7% to 11.5%) and 12.5% (95% CI 6.4% to 23.3%).

In a case series of 50 consecutive patients undergoing mesh repair of acutely incarcerated ventral or groin hernias, surgical site infection occurred in 32% of all patients (8% superficial, 24% deep or organ/space). Predictors of surgical site infection were CT evidence of fluid in the hernia sac, initial heart rate 90 beats/min or greater, and BMI of 35 kg/m or greater.

A repaired inguinal hernia is fully stable immediately after surgery and pain should be the only limiting factor for return to work or activities. There is no known association between physical activity after herniotomy and recurrence.

The risk of need for contralateral inguinal hernia repair after unilateral repair appears to be low (3.8%) after 10 years. Older men were at highest risk and half of the contralateral repairs occurred within 2.5 years. However, in a recent meta-analysis of 19 articles with a total of 277,288 patients, metachronous (separate occurrence) contralateral inguinal hernia developed in about 8.3% (95% CI 7.1%-9.5%) of patients following repair of inguinal hernia, although study heterogeneity was high.

Thirty-day mortality following inguinal hernia repair ranges from 0-11.8% for emergency repair and 0-1.7% following elective repair. This risk is estimated to be 26-fold higher for emergency repair (RR 26.0, 95% CI 21.6-31.4, I2 = 0%).

Chronic pain, attributed to entrapment of branches of the genitofemoral nerve, occurs in 1% to 19% of patients who have undergone surgical repair. In one study, chronic pain prevalence decreased substantially over the approximately 7 years of follow-up.
Up to one-fourth of these patients experience neuropathic pain, moderate to severe in nature.

Surgical options for treatment of chronic severe pain after inguinal hernia surgery include resection of entrapped nerves, mesh removal in the case of mesh-related pain and removal of fixation sutures.
Surgically-treated patients have a low incidence of recurrence between 2% and 17%, with a lower rate of recurrence in hernias repaired with mesh.

Based on a review of the Premier database of 317,636 inguinal hernia repairs and the National Surgical Quality Improvement Program database of 180,512 inguinal hernia repairs, recurrence rates for men range from 10.5% to 11.4% and for women from 6.2% to 7.1%. Using a Medicare database of elective groin hernia repair, female patients also experienced a lower risk of operative hernia recurrence at 5-year follow-up compared with males (aHR 0.7, 95% CI 0.6-0.8). However, in a meta-analysis of 29 studies including 1,236,694 patients, females were less likely to undergo minimally invasive procedures and had higher risks of recurrence (RR 1.3), chronic pain (RR 1.5), and surgical site infections (RR 1.5).
It is not clear whether occupational mechanical exposures increase risk of recurrence.

The European Registry for Abdominal Wall Hernias-Quality of Life (EuraHS-QoL) is a patient-reported outcome tool designed to assess perioperative quality of life for patients undergoing inguinal hernia repair. The minimally important differences in overall score and sub-scores are: overall 10 (range 0-90), 3 for pain domain (range 0 to 30), 5 for restriction of activities domain (range 0 to 40), and 2 for the cosmesis domain (range 0 to 20).
Hernias become symptomatic more commonly in pregnancy, usually in the first trimester.
If possible, elective repair should be delayed until after delivery.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 3 RCTs and 4 observational studies found laparoscopic herniorrhaphy to be superior to open repair of bilateral inguinal hernias with respect to shorter operative times and metachronous contralateral hernia but was similar in operative time for unilateral hernias and in length of hospital stay, recurrence, and complication rates.

In three more recent meta-analyses, one including 21 comparative studies, one including 8 RCTs with 733 children, and the third including 6 RCTs with 594 children, authors found no differences between laparoscopic and open hernia repair for most outcomes - recurrence rates, surgical time, and length of hospitalization in the first and second study and postoperative complications and time to resume full activity in the second and third study. Laparoscopic surgery was associated with increased risk of wound infection, but decreased risk of ascending testis in the first meta-analysis and was again shown to significantly reduce operative time in bilateral but not unilateral inguinal hernia vs. open surgery, but with longer time to hospital discharge in that study. Reduced risk of metachronous inguinal hernia was demonstrated in the first and third study with the laparoscopic approach, but authors noted substantial study heterogeneity making the clinical relevance of most estimated effects limited.

In a 5-year, single center case series of 380 children undergoing laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair, complication rates were similar in infants compared with older children, although there was a trend towards higher recurrence rate in older children of 4% vs. 1% for infants.

A trial randomized 338 preterm infants with inguinal hernia to early repair before NICU discharge or late repair when the infants were at least 55 weeks postmenstrual age. The late repair strategy resulted in fewer infants having at least one serious adverse event (18% vs 28%, RD 7.9%, credible interval 0% to 16.9%).
Anesthesia issues

Inguinal hernia is common among preterm infants, occurring in 38% of those whose birth weight is between 751 and 1000 g. Cochrane authors found moderate-quality evidence that administration of spinal vs. general anesthesia without pre- or intraoperative sedative administration reduced the risk of postoperative apnea in preterm infants undergoing inguinal herniorrhaphy at a postmature age. There was no difference between groups on overall incidence of postoperative apnea, bradycardia, oxygen desaturation, need for postoperative analgesics, or respiratory support.

Laryngeal mask airway use for pediatric laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair demonstrated no greater airway complications or safety risks than endotracheal tube intubation and was associated with less post-operative cough and shorter anesthesia time (WMD -6.88 min) and recovery time (WMD -4.85 min) based on 5 RCTs including 402 patients.

listitem.strong: Timing of surgery and exploration for contralateral hernia

list.listitem: Timing of surgery for inguinal hernia in preterm infants was addressed in one meta-analysis of 6 comparative studies with 1761 infants. Authors found no significant difference between pre or post-neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) discharge in incarceration rate, surgical or secondary complications. However, the odds of recurrence and respiratory difficulty was significantly increased in the early group. In a second meta-analysis, also including 6 studies, the early repair group had lower odds of developing incarceration (OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.34-0.55, I2 = 0%), but higher risk of post-operative respiratory complications (OR 4.36, 95% CI 2.13-8.94, I2 = 40%). There were no significant differences in recurrence rate or surgical complication rate between early and delayed groups.

There is controversy over whether exploration of the contralateral side should be performed in children with unilateral inguinal hernia. Authors of a meta-analysis of 7 prospective studies with 1774 children, 82% boys, found an overall incidence of metachronous contralateral inguinal hernias of 6%. The incidence was significantly higher in children with initial left-sided vs. right sided hernias (9% and 3%, respectively), in females vs. males (8% and 4%), and in children with open vs. closed contralateral processus vaginalis (14% and 3%).

With respect to later childhood development, in an RCT of 722 infants undergoing inguinal herniorrhaphy randomly allocated to awake-regional anesthesia or general anesthesia (median duration 54 minutes), of the 58% for whom outcome information was available, there were no differences in full-scale intelligence quotient on the Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence, third edition, at 5 years of age.

Among adolescents undergoing groin hernia repair, authors of a meta-analysis of 2 RCTs, six prospective, and 13 retrospective cohort studies including 3,816 patients found low incidences of recurrence for both open non-mesh (1.6%, 95% CI 0.6-2.5%) open mesh (0.6%, 95% CI 0.0-1.4%), laparoscopic non-mesh (1.9%, 95% CI 1.1-2.8%) and laparoscopic mesh repairs (no recurrences). Rates of postoperative chronic pain across all surgical types were low (0-11%).
